qs.q: A 50-year-old woman with a sedentary lifestyle and obesity develops type 2 diabetes mellitus. How is the genetic contribution to this condition best categorized in clinical genetics?
o: X-linked recessive inheritance affecting peripheral insulin receptor synthesis
Single-gene autosomal dominant transmission with incomplete adult penetrance
Mitochondrial maternal inheritance leading to progressive beta-cell failure
Multifactorial inheritance involving interactions among many susceptibility loci
Trinucleotide repeat expansion causing toxic gain of function in islets
qs.e: Type 2 diabetes is a classic multifactorial disorder shaped by numerous genetic loci and environmental factors.

qs.q: A clinical genetics resident is reviewing dysmorphology terms. What defines a malformation in morphogenesis?
o: A structural distortion caused by mechanical uterine compression
A primary error of morphogenesis where development is intrinsically abnormal
A secondary destruction of a previously normal tissue structure
A single localized defect that causes multiple downstream anomalies
qs.e: A malformation is a primary error of morphogenesis where the developmental process is intrinsically abnormal from the start. In contrast, deformations are caused by extrinsic mechanical forces.
qs.s: Clinical Genetics: Master Mendelian Disorders & Molecular Basis: MCQs

qs.q: A clinical genetics team discusses screening and diagnostic modalities for congenital anomalies. Which of the following combinations consists entirely of invasive methods of prenatal diagnosis?
o: Chorionic villous sampling with percutaneous cordocentesis
Obstetric ultrasound with chorionic villous sampling
qs.e: Chorionic villous sampling (CVS) and percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (cordocentesis) are invasive prenatal diagnostic procedures. Obstetric ultrasound and MRI are non-invasive imaging modalities.

exam: A 4‑year‑old presents with recurrent painful limb swelling and a positive family history of early deaths. What bedside steps confirm sickle cell disease and what is the next management step? — Perform a sickle‑cell solubility test; if positive, start penicillin prophylaxis and arrange referral for hydroxyurea assessment.

A couple with a previously affected child with beta‑thalassaemia asks about future pregnancies. How do you counsel them on recurrence risk and prenatal options? — Explain a 25% recurrence risk; discuss carrier testing, prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling or pre‑implantation genetic diagnosis if available.

A malaria‑endemic region reports a surge in hemolytic episodes after a new antimalarial rollout. Which genetic condition should be considered and how would you investigate? — Consider G6PD deficiency; perform a quantitative enzyme assay or, if unavailable, review drug exposure and family history.

A teenager with mild anaemia has a microcytic picture but normal iron studies. Which hereditary condition is most likely and what test confirms it? — Beta‑thalassaemia trait; confirm with haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC.

During a blood transfusion you notice the patient develops fever and back pain. Which genetic disease predisposes to such a reaction and what preventive measure is recommended? — Sickle cell disease; give pre‑transfusion hydration and consider exchange transfusion for severe crises.

A newborn screening program is unavailable. How would you identify infants at risk for sickle cell disease in a rural clinic? — Take a detailed family pedigree, look for parental sickle‑cell trait, and perform a point‑of‑care solubility test on cord blood.

Explain why iron chelation is essential in regularly transfused thalassaemia patients and name a chelator that can be used where resources are limited. — Repeated transfusions cause iron overload leading to organ damage; deferoxamine can be administered subcutaneously in low‑resource settings.

A patient on antimalarial therapy develops dark urine and jaundice. Which genetic test would you order and why? — Order a G6PD enzyme assay because oxidative drugs can trigger hemolysis in G6PD‑deficient individuals.
ai.title: Clinical Genetics
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Clinical genetics applies inheritance principles to diagnose, counsel and manage hereditary disorders, especially in low‑resource settings where testing may be limited.

b: Autosomal dominant, recessive and X‑linked patterns
Founder effects and consanguinity increase recessive disease prevalence
Environmental modifiers (e.g., malaria) influence phenotype
sections.p: Genetic disorders arise from DNA changes that can be inherited or de novo. In East Africa, common hereditary conditions include sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency and hereditary hearing loss.

b: Point mutations, deletions, duplications, repeat expansions
Mosaicism can cause variable expression
Epigenetic changes (e.g., methylation) may mimic genetic disease
sections.p: DNA encodes proteins; mutations alter protein function or expression. The clinical impact depends on gene dosage, loss‑of‑function vs gain‑of‑function, and tissue specificity.

b: Promoter mutations affect transcription rates
Splice‑site variants produce abnormal mRNA
MicroRNA dysregulation can modify disease severity
sections.p: Gene expression is controlled at transcriptional, post‑transcriptional and translational levels. Inherited regulatory variants can cause disease even with a normal coding sequence.

b: Sickle cell disease – HbS homozygosity; vaso‑occlusive crises worsened by malaria
Beta‑thalassaemia – β‑globin gene deletions; severe anaemia aggravated by iron‑deficiency
G6PD deficiency – X‑linked enzyme loss; hemolysis triggered by infections or certain herbs
sections.p: Pathogenic variants disrupt normal protein function, leading to organ‑specific or systemic disease. In low‑resource settings, co‑existing infections can exacerbate genetic disorders.

b: Family history is the cornerstone of bedside genetics
Screening of at‑risk relatives reduces morbidity (e.g., newborn sickle‑cell screening)
Genetic counselling addresses recurrence risk and reproductive options
sections.p: Recognising hereditary patterns guides investigations, informs prognosis, and enables family counselling. Early identification prevents complications and allows targeted interventions.

t.b: Detects anaemia, sickle cells or thalassaemic indices; guides need for further haemoglobin analysis
Shows sickle cells, target cells, bite cells; useful when haemoglobin electrophoresis unavailable
Confirms sickle cell disease or thalassaemia; if unavailable, use solubility test for HbS
Quantifies enzyme activity; if lab not present, rely on clinical triggers and family history
Identifies specific mutations for counselling; when not feasible, use phenotype‑based risk assessment

b: Sickle cell – hydroxyurea (if available) to raise HbF; penicillin prophylaxis for children; malaria prophylaxis; transfusion for severe crisis
Beta‑thalassaemia – regular transfusion and iron chelation; consider bone‑marrow transplant where feasible
G6PD deficiency – avoid oxidative drugs (e.g., primaquine), infections and fava beans; treat hemolysis with supportive fluids
sections.p: Treat the genetic defect when possible, otherwise focus on preventing complications and providing supportive care.

b: Sickle cell vs. iron‑deficiency anaemia – sickle cells on smear vs microcytosis
Thalassaemia vs. lead poisoning – both cause microcytic anaemia but lead has basophilic stippling
sections.p: Distinguish hereditary anaemias from acquired causes.

b: G6PD activity can be falsely normal during a hemolytic episode; repeat after recovery
Hb electrophoresis may miss low‑level HbS in newborns; repeat after 6 months
sections.p: Certain tests may be normal despite disease.

b: Always start with a three‑generation pedigree
Explain recurrence risk for autosomal recessive diseases (25% if both parents carriers)
Mention how malaria endemicity influences sickle‑cell presentation

whenToSeekHelp: Acute vaso‑occlusive crisis with severe pain or organ dysfunction
Severe hemolysis with jaundice, dark urine and renal impairment
